think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 9-year-old boy in South Africa presenting with an 8-month history of severe upper back pain, antalgic gait, and progressive thoracolumbar gibbus (kyphosis) deformity, without fever, cough, anorexia, or known infectious contacts. Plain radiographs and MRI reveal destruction of the T12 and L1 contiguous vertebral endplates with preservation of posterior elements, accompanied by a large pre-vertebral/epidural fluid collection causing spinal canal stenosis. The clinical tension is differentiating between pyogenic bacterial spondylodiscitis, a pediatric spinal malignancy (such as Ewing sarcoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, or osteosarcoma), and spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease) complicated by multidrug resistance.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Initial clinical presentation and admission workup following physical examination, baseline laboratory investigations (CBC, ESR, CRP, LFTs, HIV ELISA), superficial pus swab microscopy/culture, chest radiography, spinal plain radiographs, and spinal MRI. Confirmatory surgical spinal decompression, deep vertebral lesion biopsy, and molecular/phenotypic drug susceptibility testing begin after this point.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pyogenic spondylodiscitis was ruled out by the chronic 8-month indolent progression without acute toxic fever or leukocytosis, negative superficial bacterial cultures, and biopsy revealing chronic necrotizing granulomas with Langhans giant cells. Pediatric spinal neoplasm was ruled out by contiguous involvement across the intervertebral disc with preserved posterior elements and cold abscess formation rather than isolated malignant osteolysis. Multidrug-resistant spinal tuberculosis was confirmed by deep surgical pus culture and line-probe assay (MTBDRplus) demonstrating rifampin resistance.
case_prompt:
A 9-year-old boy was referred to an academic hospital due to an 8-month history of worsening backache, severe upper back pain, and a progressive gibbus deformity. He had no history of chronic cough, fever, loss of weight, or anorexia, and no known history of exposure to individuals with chronic infections.
On physical examination at admission, the child was ambulatory with an antalgic limp and exhibited focal tenderness over the thoracolumbar gibbus, with referred pain in the waist. He was cooperative with normal skin and no peripheral vaccination scars. Neurological examination was completely normal and intact, with preserved motor power, sensation, and reflexes in the lower extremities.
Laboratory investigations revealed a hemoglobin level of 11.5 g/dL, a normal white blood cell count, an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 18 mg/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 20 mm/hr, and alkaline phosphatase of 211 U/L. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT, 19 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST, 31 U/L) were within normal limits. HIV serology by ELISA was negative. Plain chest radiography was unremarkable.
Spinal radiographs revealed an acute kyphotic deformity at the thoracolumbar junction (T12-L1). The T12 vertebra exhibited osseous destruction with preserved posterior elements. Destruction of the L1 upper endplate and T12 lower endplate was evident, accompanied by a prominent paravertebral soft-tissue shadow indicative of an abscess.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine demonstrated an abnormal signal and destruction of T12 and L1 with narrowing and distortion of the T12-L1 intervertebral disc, accompanied by a large pre-vertebral fluid collection extending into the epidural space, displaying low signal on T1, high signal on T2, and peripheral contrast enhancement, with associated spinal canal stenosis and cord compression; posterior elements were preserved and facet joints were normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pyogenic spondylodiscitis / acute spinal osteomyelitis (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to destructive vertebral changes, paravertebral abscess formation, and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 18 mg/L). However, the patient exhibited an indolent 8-month progression without acute septic symptoms or leukocytosis, and superficial pus swabs were negative for bacterial pathogens.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He had no history of tuberculosis contact or constitutional symptoms (cough or fever, loss of weight or loss of appetite).

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pediatric spinal neoplasm (e.g., Ewing sarcoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, lymphoma)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because of a solitary destructive thoracolumbar spinal lesion leading to pathologic kyphosis in a 9-year-old child. However, the lesion involved contiguous vertebral endplates across the disc space with preserved posterior elements and extensive cold abscess formation, and biopsy revealed chronic necrotizing granulomas rather than malignancy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The pathological diagnosis of the spine (T12/L1) on the vertebral lesion biopsy revealed the presence of chronic necrotising granulomas with multinucleated Langhans-type giant cells.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The pivotal confirmatory turning point was vertebral biopsy demonstrating chronic necrotizing granulomas with Langhans-type giant cells, followed by surgical drainage of deep gibbus pus isolating Mycobacterium tuberculosis confirmed as rifampin-resistant by line-probe assay (MTBDRplus) and phenotypic MGIT drug susceptibility testing, establishing multidrug-resistant spinal tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The line-probe assay result showed rifampin monoresistance, which was later confirmed by the phenotypic MGIT 960 drug susceptibility testing as rifampin monoresistant, ethambutol resistant and isoniazid sensitive after 9 months of first-line anti-tuberculosis treatment.

editor_comments: Verified admission breakpoint strictly excludes surgical decompression, line-probe assay, MGIT culture results, and second-line MDR-TB treatment.
